### Question 1

Think of a detective walking into a room. Everything in the room is data — the rug, the lamp, the muddy footprint — but only some of it is a clue. A cue is the nursing word for a clue: a fact that actually tells you something about what is going on with the client. You gather clues first, then form ideas about what they mean, then act.

### Question 2

Imagine you are trying to find out why your bike won't roll. The color of the bike is a real fact, but it doesn't help answer your question. The flat tire does. Relevant just means "this fact helps me answer the question I'm actually asking right now" — so the very same fact can be relevant in one situation and useless in another.

### Question 3

If your friend says "my stomach hurts," that's something only they can feel, so you have to take their word for it. If you see them doubled over and feel that their forehead is hot, that's something you can check yourself. The first kind is subjective, the second is objective. Notice that neither one has to be a number, and neither one is automatically more trustworthy.

### Question 4

If a student who always scores 95 on spelling tests suddenly gets a 78, that's still a passing grade — but something changed, and it's worth asking why. Normal ranges are like "passing" for everybody in general; a baseline is that one person's usual score. Watching the change is how you catch a problem while the number still looks acceptable on paper.

### Question 5

One puzzle piece by itself tells you almost nothing. Snap a few together and suddenly you can see it's a boat — and you also notice the one piece that clearly doesn't belong. Cues work the same way: findings mean far more in groups than alone, and the piece that doesn't fit the picture is often the one worth chasing.

### Question 6

Imagine a smoke alarm that beeped at the same volume for burnt toast, an open window, and an actual fire. Pretty soon you'd stop reacting to any of it. If every odd number in a chart shouts equally loudly, the one that truly matters gets lost, and you lose the ability to tell urgent from ordinary.

### Question 7

If a friend texts "the movie was bad," you learn their verdict but nothing you can judge for yourself. If they text "it ran three hours and the sound was muffled," you can decide what you think. Charting works the same way: write what you actually saw and heard, because the next person may read those same observations and see something you missed.

### Question 8

Only one of these four facts would make a nurse stop and say "tell me more about that." Feeling dizzy on standing up is the body reporting something about blood flow. A room number is a label on a door — useful for finding the person, useless for understanding how they are doing.

### Question 9

If you're looking for a lost dog and you check the backyard and it's empty, "empty" is still useful — you now know where not to look. Normal results do the same job: they cross a possibility off the list. Crossing things off is real progress, which is why a normal result you actually reasoned with beats an abnormal one you only wrote down.

### Question 10

When something goes wrong, the two questions that narrow things fastest are "when did it start?" and "what makes it better or worse?" Those answers point toward some explanations and away from others. Knowing someone had their tonsils out at age six is a genuine fact, but it doesn't move you closer to why they can't catch their breath today.

### Question 11

Walk into a kitchen looking for a snack and you notice the fruit bowl. Walk into the same kitchen looking for your keys and you notice the cluttered counter. Same room, different things jump out, because what you're looking for shapes what you see. That's the reason experienced nurses force themselves to name a second possible explanation before settling on the first.

### Question 12

Picture reading a long email. Missing a cue is skipping the one sentence that says the meeting moved to Tuesday. Being misled by irrelevant information is spending five minutes on the quote in the sender's signature. One is failing to see what matters; the other is staring hard at what doesn't — and reading the whole email more slowly only fixes one of them.
